world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Itene/Moré is not in the catalog. Both Glottolog stress-title items are one and the same 10-page conference paper (Angenot-de Lima & Angenot, Actas III Jornadas de Lingüística Aborigen, Buenos Aires 1998 [pres. 1997], pp. 239-249); Glottolog 112532's 'Angenot & Ferrarezi' authorship is a ditto-line mis-parse of Fabre's Chapakura bibliography (Fabre PDF downloaded and saved). The Actas paper is about Proto-Chapakura stress reconstruction, relevant to Itene as the most conservative daughter, but no open copy exists anywhere I could reach (etnolinguistica.org by automated download, Crossref, archive.org; §2.2 p.24, §4.2.2 p.70; ILLA 2000 pp.156-157). Best first-hand statement read: Lima 2002 Leiden thesis §2.1.3.1 p.53 — every simple lexical word is a heavy (CVC/CVː) stressed syllable optionally preceded by one unstressed light CV syllable, i.e. weight-based, effectively fixed final, non-contrastive stress; ILLA 2000 p.156 confirms instrumentally that Moré keeps prominence 'sempre e inequivocamente na sílaba pesada'.

En d'autres termes, le mot lexical simple est donc toujours constitué d'une syllabe accentuable lourde (c'est-à-dire, à rime bimoraïque VC ou V:), éventuellement précédée d'une syllabe atone légère (c'est-à-dire, à rime monomoraïque V). [p.54:] Structure du mot lexical composé : ... soit d'une locution grammaticale lexicalisée accentuable sur la dernière syllable ... soit d'une séquence de mots simples, où l'avant-dernier mot est accentué et séparé du dernier mot par une limite interne "forte" ≠
new_statements.translation: It consists of: either /#(CV)ˈCVC#/ as in 'water', 'jaguar'; or /#(CV)ˈCVː#/ as in 'shoot with a bow', 'tree sp.'. In other words, the simple lexical word always consists of one stressable heavy syllable (i.e. with a bimoraic rhyme VC or Vː), optionally preceded by an unstressed light syllable (i.e. with a monomoraic rhyme V). [p.54:] Structure of the compound lexical word: ... either a lexicalised grammatical locution stressable on the last syllable ... or a sequence of simple words in which the penultimate word is stressed and separated from the last word by a 'strong' internal boundary ≠.
new_statements.citation: Angenot-de Lima, Geralda. 2002. Description phonologique, grammaticale et lexicale du Moré, langue amazonienne de Bolivie et du Brésil. Proefschrift, Universiteit Leiden. Tome I, ch. 2 Phonologie, §2.1.3.1 (p.53), §2.1.3.3 (p.54), §S5.1.a (p.138).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (808 pp., text layer with legacy IPA font: '»'=ˈ, '/'=ʔ, '˘'=ː) opened with extracted text. Printed p.53 (=PDF p.53), §2.1.3.1 'Structure d'un mot lexical simple': 'Elle consiste de : soit # (CV) ˈCVC # comme ˈʔkɔm.. eau, kiˈnam.. jaguar; soit # (CV) ˈCVː # comme : ˈkɔː.. tirer à l'arc, kaˈwaː.. arbre (esp.). En d'autres termes, le mot lexical simple est donc toujours constitué d'une syllabe accentuable lourde (c'est-à-dire, à rime bimoraïque VC ou V:), éventuellement précédée d'une syllabe atone légère (c'est-à-dire, à rime monomoraïque V).' -- verbatim as quoted (only the IPA examples were elided/transliterated by the first reader). p.53 §2.1.3.2 grammatical simple word likewise #ˈCV…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Moré simple words (lexical and grammatical) are maximally disyllabic, (CV).ˈCVC or (CV).ˈCVː: the final syllable is always heavy and carries the stress, a preceding light CV syllable is unstressed; stress is thus word-final and coincides with (predictable from) syllable weight, so the author treats it as non-contrastive. In compounds formed with 'weak' boundaries (lexicalised grammatical locutions) stress is on the last syllable of the whole compound; in compounds of two simple words joined by a 'strong' boundary the first (penultimate) word keeps its stress and the last word is deaccented (e.g. [ˈsɛːmɛ] 'caiman').
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described; degrees of 'accentuation' (primaire/secondaire/tertiaire) are used only as utterance-level prominence grades conditioning phonostylistic rules (pp.170ff). Acoustic means for light vs heavy syllables given p.55 (15.7 vs 27.2 dB; 40.0 vs 42.5 ST; 145 vs 234/404 ms).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds with a 'strong' internal boundary have stress on the penultimate word, so surface stress can be non-final (e.g. [ˈʔuːpʷək] 'mosquito sp.', [wɐˈɾaːsim] 'town'); a pronominalised determiner 'captures' the accent (p.138). At utterance level only one word stress keeps prominence, 'le plus souvent situé sur la syllabe finale mais cela n'est pas nécessairement le cas'; the author states the metrical system is 'non encore pleinement identifié' and quotes Gussenhoven (p.c., p.139): 'There is no satisfactory statement of Moré stress or feet'.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is for the (morpho)phonological word in hyperarticulated/citation register; in casual registers vowel shortening and fusion of monosyllabic lexemes merge several morphological words into one phonological word (ILLA 2000 pp.150-151). Utterance-level prominence treated separately (§S5.1.a).
new_statements.identity_note: Angenot-de Lima 2002 describes Moré (= Itene, ISO ite, iten1243) as spoken at Monte Azul / Vuelta Grande on the Guaporé, Beni, Bolivia (c. 2000, a few dozen active speakers). The companion MA thesis Rodrigues Duran 2000 (also saved) describes the 'Kaw Tayo'/Kujubi variety, which Glottolog lists as a separate language Kuyubi (kuyu1236), not iten1243. The ILLA 2000 and Lima 1997 works are pan-Chapakuran but report Moré-specific measurements.

[ILLA 2000 p.156:] (a) em Moré, a proeminência acentual do Protochapakura, que integra a intensidade e a altura, manteve-se sempre e inequivocamente na sílaba pesada na sua modalidade 'resistente'
new_statements.translation: Either # (CV) 'CVC # as in 'ʔɛkkɔm 'water', ki'nam 'jaguar'; or # (CV) 'CVː # as in 'kɔː 'to shoot with a bow', ka'waː 'tree (sp.)'. In other words, the simple lexical word is thus always made up of a stressable heavy syllable (i.e. with a bimoraic rhyme VC or V:), optionally preceded by an unstressed light syllable (i.e. with a monomoraic rhyme V). [ILLA 2000:] (a) in Moré, the Proto-Chapakura accentual prominence, which integrates intensity and pitch, has always and unequivocally been maintained on the heavy syllable in its 'resistant' modality.
new_statements.citation: Angenot-de Lima, Geralda. 2002. Description phonologique, grammaticale et lexicale du Moré, langue amazonienne de Bolivie et du Brésil. Proefschrift, Universiteit Leiden (2 tomes, 808 pp.). §2.1.3.1 'Structure d'un mot lexical simple', p.53 (PDF p.53). Corroborated by Angenot-de Lima & Angenot 2000, 'O sistema prosódico Panchapakura de demarcação lexical', ILLA 1: 149-164, p.156 (Moré) and p.157 (conclusions).
new_statements.reading: Moré/Itene word stress is weight-determined and, given the phonotactics, invariably word-final: a simple lexeme is monosyllabic (one heavy CVC/CVː syllable) or disyllabic (light CV + heavy CVC/CVː), and the heavy — always final — syllable carries stress and high pitch while the light initial syllable is unstressed and low. Stress is non-contrastive (predictable from weight; Lima 1997 p.24, ILLA 2000 p.157: 'o acento não é fonológico por ser previsível'). At utterance level only one primary accent survives, most often on the utterance-final syllable (Lima 2002 §S5.1.a p.138: 'L'accent primaire de l'énoncé est le plus souvent situé sur la syllabe finale mais cela n'est pas nécessairement le cas'). Coding suggestion: fixed final / weight-sensitive (heavy-final), non-lexical. The 2002 thesis is the reference grammar of Moré itself; the ILLA 2000 paper adds instrumental confirmation over 5 Chapakura languages.
